# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia and a leading cause of cardioembolic stroke. The pathophysiological basis for left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) rests on a classic observation: in a review of all relevant articles describing the site of left atrial thrombus in patients with atrial fibrillation, the thrombus was localized to the left atrial appendage in 43% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and in 91% of patients with nonrheumatic atrial fibrillation [1]. Although oral anticoagulation (OAC) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention, a substantial proportion of patients have contraindications or bleeding risks that limit its use [2]. This created the impetus for a site-specific mechanical alternative that targets the dominant source of thrombus while avoiding the bleeding hazards of chronic anticoagulation [3].

## Landmark Randomized Evidence

The first large randomized trial, PROTECT AF, compared the Watchman device against warfarin. The multicenter PROTECT AF study was conducted to determine whether percutaneous left atrial appendage closure with a filter device was noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention; 707 patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and at least one risk factor were randomized to either the Watchman device or continued warfarin in a 2:1 ratio [4]. The efficacy of percutaneous closure was non-inferior to warfarin therapy; although there was a higher rate of adverse safety events in the intervention group, these were mainly a result of periprocedural complications [5]. Subsequent analyses showed that there was a significantly higher risk of complications, predominantly pericardial effusion and procedural stroke related to air embolism, but experience improved the safety of the procedure [6]. Longer-term follow-up at 2.3 years affirmed durable efficacy and a mortality benefit [7].

Because of safety and patient-selection concerns, the confirmatory PREVAIL trial was performed. At 18 months, the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve prespecified noninferiority, while the second coprimary endpoint of stroke or systemic embolism beyond 7 days achieved noninferiority [8]. Failure to achieve noninferiority on the first endpoint may have partly been due to a lower than expected event rate in the control arm. A patient-level meta-analysis of both trials found that patients receiving LAAC with the Watchman device had significantly fewer hemorrhagic strokes and lower cardiovascular/unexplained death [9]. The 5-year pooled outcomes concluded that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke, and mortality [10], and a net-clinical-benefit analysis quantified these tradeoffs favorably [11].

## Patients Ineligible for Anticoagulation

For patients unable to take OAC, the ASAP study enrolled 150 patients with nonvalvular AF and CHADS2 score ≥1 who were considered ineligible for warfarin [12], demonstrating that closure could be performed with antiplatelet therapy alone. Real-world experience from the EWOLUTION registry [13], which evaluated more than 1,000 patients, reinforced high implant success and an observed ischemic stroke rate substantially below predicted risk [14].

## Comparisons With Direct Oral Anticoagulants

As DOACs supplanted warfarin, head-to-head comparison became essential. The PRAGUE-17 trial randomized a total of 402 high-risk AF patients (average CHA2DS2-VASc 4.7, HAS-BLED 3.1); after a 3.5-year median follow-up, LAAC was noninferior to DOACs for the primary endpoint [15]. In the prespecified 4-year analysis, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [16].

The OPTION trial addressed the post-ablation population. Researchers randomized 1,360 patients with AF and elevated CHA2DS2-VASc to either ablation plus LAAC or ablation plus oral anticoagulation, with closure performed concomitantly or sequentially [17]. LAAO was noninferior to OAC for the composite primary endpoint of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and was superior to OAC for non–procedure-related bleeding [18].

## Device Evolution and Procedural Considerations

LAAC devices have evolved considerably. The next-generation Watchman FLX was evaluated in the PINNACLE FLX trial, a single-arm, nonrandomized trial at 29 U.S. sites with 400 patients [19], meeting its safety and efficacy endpoints, with sustained 2-year outcomes [20]. The Amulet IDE trial provided the first large head-to-head device comparison; the Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder and decreased with operator experience [21]. Five-year results confirmed long-term safety of both devices [22]. Procedural planning relies on transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac CT for anatomical sizing and transseptal access [23], and the Amplatzer cardiac plug provided early European procedural experience [24].

## Complications and Antithrombotic Management

Device-related thrombus (DRT) remains an important concern. In a pooled analysis of four FDA trials, Dukkipati and colleagues reported that DRT formed on the left atrial face of the device and was associated with thromboembolism [25,26], with a pooled DRT incidence near 3.7% that predicted subsequent stroke [27]. Bleeding outcomes after closure compare favorably with long-term warfarin in pooled patient-level analyses [28]. Post-implantation regimens have varied from warfarin-bridging to dual antiplatelet therapy, and remain individualized by bleeding risk [29].

## Surgical Context and Conclusions

The surgical LAAOS III trial demonstrated that among patients with AF who had undergone cardiac surgery, most of whom continued antithrombotic therapy, the risk of ischemic stroke or systemic embolism was lower with concomitant left atrial appendage occlusion than without it [30], underscoring that appendage exclusion provides protection additive to anticoagulation. Taken together, percutaneous LAAC has matured from a warfarin alternative into a validated therapy—noninferior to both warfarin and DOACs in randomized trials—particularly valuable for patients with bleeding risks or anticoagulation intolerance, while DRT, peridevice leak, and optimal antithrombotic strategy remain active areas of investigation.
